--- jupyter: stats --- # Clustering {#sec-clustering} Clustering is an unsupervised learning problem. We observe only a predictor matrix $$ X= \mqty[ x_1^\top\\ \vdots\\ x_n^\top ] \in\mathbb R^{n\times p}, $$ and try to divide the observations into groups whose members are similar. Unlike classification, there are no training labels that define the correct groups. Clustering is commonly used to: - explore unknown subpopulations; - summarize a large dataset by a small number of prototypes; - organize observations for visualization; - generate hypotheses for later scientific analysis. ::: {.callout-caution} ## A cluster is not automatically a real class A clustering algorithm always returns a partition when asked to do so. The result may reflect scientific structure, but it may also reflect scaling, outliers, an unsuitable distance, or a forced choice of the number of clusters. Interpretation is part of the analysis. ::: Most clustering methods begin with a notion of dissimilarity. For numerical features, the default is often Euclidean distance: $$ d(x_i,x_j) = \norm{x_i-x_j}_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{\ell=1}^p(x_{i\ell}-x_{j\ell})^2}. $$ The distance defines what the algorithm means by *similar*. Changing the features, their scales, or the distance metric itself effectively changes the clustering problem. In particular, features with larger numerical ranges can dominate the Euclidean distance calculation. Therefore, as with KNN and other distance-based algorithms, it is often necessary to standardize or normalize the features so that they are on a comparable scale before performing clustering. ::: {.callout-note} ## Scaling is a modeling decision Standardize when numerical scales are arbitrary or incomparable. Do not standardize automatically when the original magnitude is scientifically meaningful, such as comparable pixel intensities or measurements already expressed on a common scale. ::: Euclidean distance is not the only choice. Manhattan distance can be more robust to a few large coordinate differences, cosine distance focuses on direction rather than magnitude, and domain-specific data may require a custom dissimilarity. The distance must match the question being asked. ## K-Means Clustering K-means represents every cluster by its center. Let $C_1,\ldots,C_K$ be a partition of the observations, and let $$ \mu_k=\frac{1}{|C_k|}\sum_{i\in C_k}x_i $$ be the center of cluster $k$. ::: {#def-kmeans} ## K-means objective K-means chooses the partition that minimizes the within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS): $$ \operatorname{WCSS} = \sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in C_k}\norm{x_i-\mu_k}_2^2. $$ It is also called **inertia** in some references. ::: The standard algorithm alternates between two steps: 1. assign each observation to its nearest center; 2. replace each center by the mean of its assigned observations. Each step decreases, or leaves unchanged, the K-means objective. The algorithm eventually reaches a local optimum, but not necessarily the global optimum. For this reason, software usually tries several random initializations. ### A Simulated Example We use `make_blobs` from `sklearn.datasets` to create a datasets, with 500 observations, 3 true centers and the standard deviation of each cluster is 0.7, 0.9 and 0.8. The dataset has 2 features, for the purpose of easy visualization. ::: {#bf8fbd8a .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs X, true_group = make_blobs( n_samples=500, n_features=2, centers=3, cluster_std=[0.7, 0.9, 0.8], random_state=4 ) ``` ::: The dataset looks like this, with colors indicates the true class. ::: {#06bc782e .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt plt.scatter(X[:, 0], X[:, 1], c=true_group) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](cluster_files/figure-html/cell-3-output-1.png){width=570 height=411} ::: ::: We can use `KMeans` from `sklearn.cluster` to implement the K-means model. The API is very similar to supervised learning `sklearn` API. In addition, you can now use `.fit_predict()` to fit and then predict on the same data `X`. Note that the argument `n_init` is to set the number of random initializations. The K-means algorithm will be run `n_init` times, and the best result in terms of inertia will be reported. ::: {#57960cd1 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} from sklearn.cluster import KMeans kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=3, n_init=20, random_state=1) cluster = kmeans.fit_predict(X) plt.scatter(X[:, 0], X[:, 1], c=cluster) plt.scatter( kmeans.cluster_centers_[:, 0], kmeans.cluster_centers_[:, 1], marker="X", color="black", label="centers", ) plt.xlabel("x1") plt.ylabel("x2") plt.title("K-Means Clustering") plt.legend(); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](cluster_files/figure-html/cell-4-output-1.png){width=589 height=449} ::: ::: The fitted centers are available from the model. ::: {#b9539b8c .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} kmeans.cluster_centers_ ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` array([[ 9.45999811, 1.0020861 ], [ 3.95212561, -5.72057393], [ 9.54129566, 4.35377553]]) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## Label switching Cluster labels are arbitrary. A cluster labeled `0` in one fit may be labeled `2` in another fit even when the two partitions are identical. Interpret the groups through their members and feature summaries, not the numeric label. ::: ### What K-Means Assumes Because K-means uses squared Euclidean distance to a center, it is most effective when clusters are: - compact and approximately spherical; - separated by their centers; - reasonably similar in size and spread; - not dominated by extreme outliers. It can fail on curved clusters, clusters with very different densities, or data where a mean is not an appropriate prototype. ::: {#c9cb25ca .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} from sklearn.datasets import make_circles X_circle, y_circle = make_circles( n_samples=500, factor=0.45, noise=0.05, random_state=1 ) circle_kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=2, n_init=20, random_state=1) circle_cluster = circle_kmeans.fit_predict(X_circle) fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4), sharex=True, sharey=True) axs[0].scatter(X_circle[:, 0], X_circle[:, 1], c=y_circle, s=18) axs[0].set_title("True labels") axs[1].scatter(X_circle[:, 0], X_circle[:, 1], c=circle_cluster, s=18) axs[1].set_title("K-Means Partition") for ax in axs: ax.set_xlabel("x1") ax.set_ylabel("x2") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](cluster_files/figure-html/cell-6-output-1.png){width=823 height=376} ::: ::: K-means separates the plane into convex regions, so it cannot recover the two rings. It requires other methods to deal with these types of data. ### Internal Evaluation a Clustering Without known labels, clustering evaluation must combine several kinds of evidence. Internal metrics assess geometric compactness and separation, stability checks whether the result persists under perturbations, and interpretation determines whether the groups are meaningful in the original problem. Internal clustering metrics evaluate a partition using only the observations and their assigned clusters. They can compare values of $K$, initializations, or different clustering methods, provided that the same features, scaling, and distance are used. No single metric defines the correct clustering. Each metric favors a particular geometric idea of a good partition. For simplicity we only cover WCSS and the Silhouette score in the notes. #### Within-Cluster Sum of Squares The K-means objective is the within-cluster sum of squares: $$ \operatorname{WCSS} = \sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in C_k}\norm{x_i-\mu_k}_2^2. $$ In `sklearn`, WCSS is called **inertia** and is stored in `inertia_`. ::: {#bb7e19ab .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} kmeans.inertia_ ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` 569.9430376800667 ``` ::: ::: Smaller inertia means observations are closer to their assigned centers. However, inertia cannot be compared naively across different values of $K$: it always decreases when more clusters are added and becomes zero when every distinct observation is its own cluster. #### Silhouette Value The silhouette value evaluates both within-cluster cohesion and separation from neighboring clusters. For observation $i$, define: - $a(i)$ as its average distance to observations in its own cluster; - $b(i)$ as the smallest average distance to any other cluster. The silhouette value is $$ s(i)=\frac{b(i)-a(i)}{\max\{a(i),b(i)\}}. $$ It lies between $-1$ and $1$: - values near $1$ indicate a well-separated observation; - values near $0$ indicate an observation near a cluster boundary; - negative values suggest that another cluster may be closer. The overall silhouette score is the average of $s(i)$ over all observations. Larger values are preferred. It requires at least two clusters and is available as `silhouette_score()`. ### External Evaluation a Clustering If known labels exist, they may be used after fitting for evaluation. The adjusted Rand index compares two partitions while accounting for agreement expected by chance. ::: {#4374e6c3 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_rand_score adjusted_rand_score(true_group, cluster) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` 0.9702725900485715 ``` ::: ::: This does not turn clustering into supervised learning: the labels were not used to fit the clusters. ### Choosing the Number of Clusters The number of clusters $K$ is a tuning parameter. There is no universally correct criterion because the useful level of grouping depends on the scientific question. The following example compares the four internal metrics over a range of candidate values using K-means. Inertia is also defined for $K=1$, while the other metrics require at least two clusters. ::: {#27de18da .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd from sklearn.metrics import ( silhouette_score, calinski_harabasz_score, davies_bouldin_score, ) k_values = range(2, 11) metric_rows = [] for k in k_values: model = KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init=20, random_state=1) labels = model.fit_predict(X) metric_rows.append( { "K": k, "inertia": model.inertia_, "silhouette": silhouette_score(X, labels), "calinski_harabasz": calinski_harabasz_score(X, labels), "davies_bouldin": davies_bouldin_score(X, labels), } ) metric_df = pd.DataFrame(metric_rows).set_index("K") metric_df ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ```{=html}

For the other metrics, we look for a maximum or minimum as indicated above. Agreement among several metrics is useful evidence, but disagreement is common because the metrics formalize different notions of cluster quality. ::: {.callout-caution} ## Diagnostics do not define the scientific answer These metrics evaluate geometric compactness and separation under the chosen features, scaling, and distance. They do not show that the clusters are stable, scientifically meaningful, or useful for a later decision. ::: ### Stability A useful clustering should not change completely after a small perturbation. A practical stability analysis can: 1. resample observations or features; 2. repeat preprocessing and clustering; 3. compare which pairs of observations are repeatedly grouped together; 4. inspect clusters that split or disappear. Instability may indicate weak separation, an unsuitable tuning choice, or insufficient data. It can also reveal that several clusterings are similarly plausible. ### Interpretation in the Original Features An embedding plot is useful, but clusters should ultimately be described using the original variables. ::: {#9ca48166 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} cluster_summary = ( pd.DataFrame(X, columns=["x1", "x2"]) .assign(cluster=cluster) .groupby("cluster") .agg(["mean", "std", "size"]) ) cluster_summary ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: For real data, combine such summaries with domain knowledge and representative observations from each group. ## Hierarchical Clustering Hierarchical clustering builds a nested sequence of partitions. Agglomerative hierarchical clustering begins with each observation in its own cluster and repeatedly merges the two closest clusters until all observations belong to one cluster. The result is a tree called a **dendrogram**. Unlike K-means, the tree can be fit before choosing the final number of clusters. ### Linkage The distance between individual observations is not enough; the algorithm also needs a distance between groups. For two clusters $G$ and $H$: **Single linkage** uses the closest pair: $$ d_{\text{single}}(G,H) = \min_{i\in G,\;j\in H}d(x_i,x_j). $$ **Complete linkage** uses the farthest pair: $$ d_{\text{complete}}(G,H) = \max_{i\in G,\;j\in H}d(x_i,x_j). $$ **Average linkage** uses the average pairwise distance: $$ d_{\text{average}}(G,H) = \frac{1}{|G||H|} \sum_{i\in G}\sum_{j\in H}d(x_i,x_j). $$ **Ward linkage** merges the pair that produces the smallest increase in within-cluster sum of squares. Different linkage rules express different ideas of what makes two groups close. Single linkage can identify elongated connected groups but is sensitive to chains of intermediate points. Complete and Ward linkage tend to produce more compact groups. ### Dendrogram ::: {#cb565b7f .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import linkage, dendrogram, fcluster X_small = X[:40] Z = linkage(X_small, method="ward") plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5)) dendrogram(Z) plt.xlabel("observation") plt.ylabel("merge height") plt.title("Hierarchical Clustering Dendrogram"); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](cluster_files/figure-html/cell-12-output-1.png){width=808 height=453} ::: ::: The merge height records the dissimilarity at which two branches are joined. A horizontal cut through the tree produces a partition. ::: {#014a9aa5 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} hierarchical_cluster = fcluster(Z, t=3, criterion="maxclust") hierarchical_cluster ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ``` array([1, 3, 3, 3, 2, 3, 2, 3, 3, 1, 1, 2, 1, 3, 1, 2, 2, 3, 2, 3, 1, 1, 3, 1, 3, 2, 1, 3, 2, 3, 3, 1, 1, 2, 1, 3, 1, 3, 3, 3], dtype=int32) ``` ::: ::: The dendrogram describes the fitted hierarchy, not uncertainty about the hierarchy. A large vertical gap can suggest a useful cut, but it is still a heuristic. ### Comparing Linkages ::: {#2e0e31b3 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} from sklearn.cluster import AgglomerativeClustering methods = ["single", "complete", "average", "ward"] fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10, 8), sharex=True, sharey=True) for ax, method in zip(axs.ravel(), methods): model = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=3, linkage=method) labels = model.fit_predict(X) ax.scatter(X[:, 0], X[:, 1], c=labels, s=18) ax.set_title(method) ax.set_xlabel("x1") ax.set_ylabel("x2") plt.tight_layout(); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](cluster_files/figure-html/cell-14-output-1.png){width=949 height=758} ::: ::: Hierarchical clustering is especially useful when the nesting itself is interesting, such as organizing genes, documents, or related products. However, early agglomerative merges cannot be undone, so a poor early merge affects the rest of the tree. ## Practical Workflow A defensible clustering analysis usually follows these steps: 1. select features that match the scientific question; 2. handle missing values and obvious data quality problems; 3. choose scaling and a distance metric deliberately; 4. visualize the data, possibly after PCA; 5. compare multiple clustering methods and tuning choices; 6. check stability under perturbations; 7. interpret the groups in the original feature space. PCA and other dimension-reduction methods are discussed in @sec-unsupervised-pca and @sec-embedding. They can reveal structure and reduce noise, but they also change the geometry on which clustering is based. ## Summary K-means minimizes within-cluster squared distance and works best for compact, center-separated groups. Hierarchical clustering builds a dendrogram and depends on both the observation distance and the linkage rule. In both cases, scaling, tuning, stability, and interpretation are part of the model rather than optional cleanup steps.
